# Temperare documentation map

Temperare checks code against the rules a repository has chosen to enforce, and reports what it finds. It is a
command-line program, `temperare`, short name `tm`. It runs clippy, SwiftLint, ruff, ast-grep, ShellCheck, pylint,
clang-tidy, golangci-lint, gitleaks, cargo-audit, vulture and Periphery as programs, reads
their output into one report, and never edits code. This file routes people and AI agents to the maintained
sources.

## Start here

- Product overview, install, first run, commands: README.md
- AI-assisted explanation, install and use: AI_START_HERE.md
- Documentation index: docs/README.md
- Changes by version: CHANGELOG.md

## Reference

- The rule file, temperare.toml, every key, the baseline sets and [[override]]: docs/reference/RULE_FILE.md
- Text output, JSON output, exit codes, the next line: docs/reference/OUTPUT.md
- Each engine: the exact command line, what check means, not available and failed: docs/reference/ENGINES.md

## Policy

- What Temperare runs, what the rule file can make it do, how to report a vulnerability: SECURITY.md
- Layout of the code, build and test commands, what a change must keep: CONTRIBUTING.md
- License: MIT, in LICENSE.

## Facts an agent needs before running it

- Commands: tm check, tm rules, tm baseline test, tm install, tm uninstall, tm help, tm --version.
- tm check [--rules <path>] [--base <rev>] [--kind quality|security] [--json] [<path>...]
- tm rules [--rules <path>] [--json]
- tm rules --loosened --base <rev> [--rules <path>] [--json]: compares the rule file as committed at <rev> with the
  working file, baseline sets included, and lists each loosening as {kind, about, before, after}: rule_gone,
  rule_not_applicable, severity_lowered, path_removed, paths_limited, exclude_added, kit_removed, kits_limited,
  outside_kit_added, exception_added, expiry_later, expiry_dropped, set_dropped, set_older. Runs no engine. Exits 0
  nothing loosened; 1 something did; 2 a usage error, a --base that names no commit or has no such rule file, or a
  problem in either file. --loosened and --base come together.
- tm baseline test [--set <name@version>] [--json]: tests each rule of the baseline sets built into tm (with no
  --set the ready ones, house@1 then standard@1; --set names one set, such as standard@1) on its failing case
  (exactly the expected finding) and its passing case (no finding), each in a throwaway git repository. A rule
  holds, is broken, not available or not applicable (a rule that requires a param its case does not give). Each
  case runs with the params it gives over the rule's own. Exits 0
  all hold; 1 a rule is broken; 2 used wrongly or an unknown set or version; 3 nothing broke but a rule was not available or
  not applicable.
- The rule file is --rules <path>, else temperare.toml at the top of the git repository.
- Baseline sets are rules built into tm. A rule file takes one with the top-level key
  baseline = ["name@version", ...], each set once. standard@1 is ready: 53 rules, all kind quality and severity
  warning, in this order: dead code (5), deprecated calls (1), suppressions written in the code (11), then
  complexity, nesting, dbg! and print, bare and blind except and commented-out code (8), then what a change adds
  (28, each only_with_base: under not_applicable without --base). house@1 is ready too: 36 rules, all kind quality,
  30 at warning and 6 at error. Five of them require params (entity_types, own_package) that the rule file gives in
  an [[override]]; until it does they are not applicable. A file may take both sets.
- A set's rules come first, in baseline order and each set's own order, then the file's own. tm rules lists them
  that way; nothing names a rule's set. A set rule's id starts with tm-, and an own rule's id may not.
- [[override]] changes one set rule: rule (its id, required) and any of severity, off = true (the rule is left out:
  not run, not listed), paths, exclude (each in place of the set's) and params (laid over the set's, key by key). One
  [[override]] per rule; one that names no rule of a taken set is a problem. An [[exception]] may name a set rule.
- A set rule can require params (none of standard@1 does). Until an [[override]] gives each one in its params the
  rule is not run, and tm rules and tm check --json list it under not_applicable, not among the rules
  ("required params not given: <names>; give them in the params of an [[override]] for "<rule id>""). A set may
  type a required param as a string or a list of strings; an [[override]] that gives it as another type is a
  problem, exit 2.
- A set's ast-grep rules carry their YAML inside tm: their check is not a path in the repository and no file is
  read for it.
- The rules of a set: tm rules on a rule file that takes it, or crates/rules/baseline/<name>/<version>/set.toml.
- --json prints one JSON object on one line on stdout, with exit and next beside the result.
- tm install [--no-place] [--short-name] [--target claude,codex,cursor] [--mode skill] [--location local] [-y]
- tm install copies the binary to ~/.local/bin/temperare, links tm beside it, writes a skill file for the harnesses
  chosen, and records what it placed in ~/.local/state/temperare/installed. tm uninstall removes what that record
  names. Both exit 0 when done, 1 when a step failed, 2 when used wrongly.
- Exit codes of tm check: 0 nothing to refuse; 1 a quality error was found; 2 used wrongly or the rule file has a
  problem, nothing checked; 3 a rule was not available; 4 the only errors are security findings, which never
  refuse; 5 a rule failed; 6 a rule of the repository's own covers nothing. The first of 2, 1, 5, 3, 4, 6 that
  applies wins.
- Exit 0 means every rule ran or is listed under not_applicable. Exit 4 means the same, except that a rule may cover
  nothing (4 ranks above 6). Exit 1 does not: read counts.not_available, counts.failed and counts.covers_nothing.
- A rule that covers none of the files git lists in the rule file's folder (tracked files in the work tree, and
  untracked files git does not ignore), or a ShellCheck rule that covers none of the scripts there, or a
  cargo-audit rule whose folder has no Cargo.lock it covers, or a clang-tidy rule that covers none of the C-family
  sources there, runs nothing,
  and whether its engine is installed does not change its result (the engine is still asked its version for the
  engines list). One of the repository's own rules is then listed as covers nothing: a "covers nothing: <rule>
  (<engine>)" line, covers_nothing in JSON ({rule, engine}), counts.covers_nothing, and exit 6, with next "fix the
  paths of each rule that covers nothing above, or remove it from <rule file>" (under --json, "fix the paths of
  each rule in covers_nothing, or remove it from <rule file>"). A baseline set's rule is listed under
  not_applicable instead, with why "its paths match no file in the rule file's folder" (ShellCheck, cargo-audit and
  clang-tidy: "no file its engine checks"). When git cannot list the files, no rule is settled this way except a
  cargo-audit rule, whose Cargo.lock tm looks for on disk once the rule file's folder is found.
- --base <rev> keeps only findings on lines added since that commit. A rule with only_with_base = true reports only
  what a change adds: without --base it reports nothing and is listed under not_applicable ("reports only what a
  change adds; run with --base"). not_applicable is never a finding and never "not available". In text, tm check
  gives not-applicable rules only as a count ("P not applicable" on the counts line), with no line per rule; --json
  lists each with its rule, engine and why. tm rules lists them too, without running an engine: "not applicable
  (P):", one "<rule>  <engine>  <why>" line each (JSON not_applicable and rules_not_applicable). It lists baseline
  rules only (a repository's own no-file rule covers nothing instead), never a rule an [[override]] turned off,
  and an only_with_base rule only when it covers no file.
- Exit 3 and exit 5 are never clean: the code was not fully checked.
- A rule fails (exit 5) when its engine gives no answer that can be read, or when its check cannot be matched back
  to findings: a clippy lint group, SwiftLint's custom_rules, a ruff rule name in place of a code, an ast-grep rule
  file outside the rule file's folder, a shellcheck check that is not one code, a git check other than test_ratio,
  a pylint check that is not one message id or is an old id pylint renamed, a clang-tidy check that is not one
  check name, a golangci-lint check with a part that is not a linter name or is typecheck, a gitleaks check with an
  empty or ALL part, a cargo-audit check that is not an advisory id or a kind, or is yanked, a vulture check that is
  not one vulture code, a periphery check that is not a Periphery result hint or all. A cargo-audit rule also
  fails when cargo-audit applied an audit.toml (its report's settings differ from the defaults), and a gitleaks rule
  before gitleaks runs when the config gitleaks reads (or a file it extends) declares an allowlist or does not parse,
  or the folder's .gitleaksignore lists anything: exceptions live in the rule file only.
  It fails too on a param its engine does not take, or a bad value: clippy
  takes allow, and max_nesting (1-1000) with check clippy::excessive_nesting; swiftlint takes max_complexity
  (1-1000) with check cyclomatic_complexity, or max_lines (1-100000) with check file_length; ruff takes
  max_complexity (1-1000) with check C901; ast-grep takes the names its YAML has as {{name}}, and count
  ("setup-vs-tests") with shared_setup (a list of globs); git takes max_ratio (0.1-100), floor (0-100000) and
  test_paths (a list of globs), all three required; shellcheck, pylint, clang-tidy, golangci-lint, gitleaks,
  cargo-audit, vulture, periphery and tessera take none. A threshold wins
  over the rule's config, and no config file of the repository is changed. The reason is in failed[].stderr_tail.
- A rule tm can refuse from the rule file alone fails whether or not its engine is installed: every check and param
  above, except the clippy lint group, an ast-grep rule file that is missing, cannot be read, or leads out of the
  folder through a symlink, and ast-grep's {{name}} params, which are refused only in the run. An ast-grep check that
  is absolute or whose .. climbs above the rule file's folder is refused from the text alone. The order a rule
  settles in: refused, then covers no file, then needs a base, then not available, then the run (docs/reference/ENGINES.md).
- A check the installed clippy, swiftlint, ruff, pylint, clang-tidy, golangci-lint or gitleaks does not know (a
  misspelt name, or one newer than the engine), or an advisory id cargo-audit's local advisory database does not
  hold, is not available (exit 3), with a why naming the engine, its version and the check. ShellCheck is not asked: a shellcheck code not on tm's built-in list of ShellCheck 0.11.0's 510 codes is
  not available ("<check> is not in temperare's list of shellcheck codes (taken from shellcheck 0.11.0)").
- check, by engine: clippy, one lint or warnings; swiftlint, one rule identifier; ruff, a rule code, a code prefix,
  ALL, or several joined by commas; ast-grep, the path of a rule file inside the rule file's folder; shellcheck, one
  code such as SC2086; git, test_ratio; pylint, one message id such as C0121; clang-tidy, one check name such as
  bugprone-branch-clone; golangci-lint, linter names such as staticcheck or staticcheck,govet; gitleaks, rule ids
  such as aws-access-token, one or several joined by commas; cargo-audit, an advisory id such as RUSTSEC-2023-0071
  or a kind: vulnerability, unmaintained, unsound, notice or all; vulture, one code V101 to V107 or V201; periphery,
  one result hint (unused, assignOnlyProperty, redundantProtocol, redundantConformance,
  redundantPublicAccessibility, superfluousIgnoreCommand) or all.
- A clippy rule needs cargo-clippy and clippy-driver on PATH; a golangci-lint rule needs golangci-lint and go; a
  shellcheck or clang-tidy rule needs git too, which lists the files; a periphery rule needs periphery and swift,
  and a Package.swift at or above the rule file's folder (an Xcode project is not available: "no Package.swift at or
  above the rule file's folder: Periphery builds the project, and tm runs it only on a Swift package").
- A clang-tidy rule needs a compile_commands.json or compile_flags.txt at or above each source; without one it is
  not available. Without a config, clang-tidy reads no .clang-tidy and ShellCheck no .shellcheckrc.
- golangci-lint runs with GOTOOLCHAIN=local, GOPROXY=off and GOSUMDB=off and GOFLAGS removed: go downloads
  nothing and writes nothing to go.mod or go.sum.
- gitleaks runs as gitleaks dir with --redact; every finding's what is tm's fixed text "gitleaks found a secret
  here; tm does not print it", and only gitleaks' error lines of stderr are kept, so the secret never reaches the
  report. GITLEAKS_CONFIG and GITLEAKS_CONFIG_TOML are removed for the run, and --ignore-gitleaks-allow makes a
  gitleaks:allow comment silence nothing. gitleaks' default skipped paths (such as .svg files and package-lock.json)
  are its stock check, not an exception.
- vulture runs as vulture --config=/dev/null [--exclude=<what git ignores>] . in the rule file's folder, so
  [tool.vulture] in pyproject.toml is not read and git-ignored Python files and folders (a virtualenv) are not
  scanned; outside a git repository the whole folder is. The rule's paths and exclude only drop findings after the
  scan. An ignored path holding a comma, or too many ignored paths for one argument, fails the rule before vulture
  runs. It still honours a # noqa on an item's line (standard@1's tm-python-suppression reports every noqa) and a
  whitelist module in the repository. Its findings have a line and no column.
- periphery builds the Swift package (the nearest Package.swift at or above the rule file's folder, no higher than
  the git top) with swift in a temporary folder tm removes after (nothing built in the repository). Before building
  it reads the manifest of the package and of each local package it reaches: a source-control or registry
  dependency or a binary target with a url anywhere, or a local package that does not resolve or lies outside the
  repository, makes the rule not available. It passes an empty --config so .periphery.yml is not read. It still
  honours // periphery:ignore and // periphery:override comments, which no released baseline set reports.
  Periphery 3.8.0 credits a top-level reference in main.swift to the nearest declaration above it, so when that
  declaration is unused the function it calls reads unused too; put top-level code first, or declarations in other
  files. A clippy or periphery rule builds the code.
- cargo-audit reads only the Cargo.lock in the rule file's folder, with --no-fetch and --no-yanked against the
  advisory database already at $CARGO_HOME/advisory-db (else $HOME/.cargo/advisory-db); tm never fetches it. With
  no database there the rule is not available, and the why names `cargo audit update-db --db <db>`. Every finding
  is on Cargo.lock with no line.
- Every finding's path is relative to the rule file's folder.
- A finding has: rule, engine, kind, severity, owner (when the rule file names one), path, line (always present;
  null when the finding has no line, as cargo-audit's on Cargo.lock), col (when the engine gives one), what (the
  engine's message), fix (the rule's fix text).
- An exception is an [[exception]] table in the rule file with rule, path, reason and approved. It records a
  person's approval. An agent does not add one on its own. An optional expires = "YYYY-MM-DD" is its last day (UTC):
  from the day after, it silences nothing and tm check lists it as expired: an "expired: <rule> <path> (expired
  <YYYY-MM-DD>)" line, expired in JSON ({rule, path, what|null, expires, reason, approved}) and counts.expired.
  Exceptions in force counts only the exceptions not expired, in tm check and tm rules alike; tm rules lists the
  expired ones apart (expired and exceptions_expired in JSON, each with expires).

## What it does not do

- It does not parse code, fix code or format code.
- It does not decide what a finding blocks.
- It does not install the engines.
- A check reads nothing back between runs; it only appends a line to its savings log
  (~/.local/state/temperare/savings.jsonl). Temperare has no network code of its own. The engines it runs are
  separate programs.
- When an engine ran, tm check's text output opens with an estimate of the tokens saved against the engines' raw
  output, ending in an ask to the agent to tell the user the turn's total; --json carries it as "saved", and
  savings_line = false in ~/.config/temperare/config.toml turns the line off.
- Rules with engine = "tessera" are accepted and, when they cover a file and have no params, are reported "not
  available" today, whether or not Tessera is installed. A Tessera rule with a param fails (exit 5).
- Rules with engine = "eslint", "mypy", "pmd", "detekt", "rubocop", "phpstan", "dart", "markdownlint", "yamllint",
  "actionlint", "hadolint", "vale", "stylelint" or "sqlfluff" are accepted and, when they cover a file, reported "not available" (no adapter for <engine> in this build) until each adapter lands, whether
  or not the engine is installed.
- Rules with engine = "git" (check test_ratio) count the lines a change adds against the commit tm check --base
  names; ast-grep rules with params.count count each file's setup and test lines whole, reporting the files the
  change adds lines to. Without --base such a rule is "not available" ("reports only what a change adds; run with
  --base") when its engine is on PATH.
- Any of these with only_with_base = true, run without --base, is listed under not_applicable instead, as any such
  rule is.

## Version note

This is version 0.4.0, built from source. There are no release downloads. It is built and accepted on macOS; Linux
and Windows are untested.
